title: Millbind
concept: A yard of pins holds real meshing gears, and the game is played inside two facts of engineering: meshed gears turn opposite ways, and a loop with an odd number of them cannot turn at all. Each player owns one furrowed millstone gear standing on the yard's rim; a single crank gear is the only power in the box and it moves to a new rim pin at the start of every round, chosen by whoever leads that round. A turn is placing one gear — low-toothed, high-toothed, or a full-height tandem that bridges both heights — then turning the crank a quarter turn to prove you have not just bound the whole yard solid; at the end of the round the crank goes round once for real and only the mills that come up turning clockwise are grinding.
novelty: Scoring is by rotation DIRECTION, not connection: a mill pays out only when an odd number of gears stands between it and a power source that relocates every round, and the illegal move is defined by physics rather than by a rule — close an odd loop and the assembly seizes in your hand, which is the legality test. Two isolated tooth-height tiers, bridged only by the scarce full-height tandem gears and by the mills and crank themselves, mean the crank's rim pin also chooses which HALF of the yard is alive at all. Searches run (all via WebSearch, per prior_art_search.sh): the mechanism verbatim ('players place meshing gears on a pin grid and an odd loop physically jams the whole train'), the object as its own pitch ('board game with real interlocking gears players place on a peg board rotation direction scoring'), the theme+mechanism combination ('gear placement board game watermill grain mill players connect gears to their millstone rotation direction'), the engineering fact as a game rule ('gear train parity odd number of gears in a loop locks up game mechanic tabletop'), and the plain title ('Millbind board game', 'Millbind OR Mill Bind game BoardGameGeek'). Closest SHIPPED comparable: Fifth Gear (Talicor, BGG 125800) — a platform of pegs and 25 real interlocking gears where you roll two d12s and race to interlock five gears of YOUR COLOUR with a central white gear. It is dice-driven, colour-owned, and purely a connection race: no rotation direction, no jam, and the white gear never moves. Gearworks (Piecekeeper Games) turned up repeatedly and is a card/marker game — gears are iconography, nothing physically meshes. Gearplexed (Steam) is a video-game puzzle that uses lockup, not a tabletop product. The nearest thing found to a jam-as-attack is Factory Floor Wars, a Purdue toy-design student prize entry (connect your two fixed gears while jamming the opponent, cogs on a grid, stacking and belts) — treat as INCONCLUSIVE/PARTIAL: it is a student project, not a shipped game, and no published rules confirm parity, direction-based scoring or a relocatable drive. The title returned no game; 'Mill' alone is Nine Men's Morris, which the compound does not read as. Note that Fifth Gear's whole ownership scheme is colour, which this pipeline cannot print — Millbind carries ownership on hub prisms instead.

art_direction.form_language: Cast-iron mill gearing on a plank floor: heavy chamfered gear rims, thick spoked webs with big round lightening holes, nothing thinner than a finger. The board is a slab of milled floor with raised plank ribs and a chamfered skirt, bristling with stubby pins. Everything reads as machined and greased, not printed — no filigree, no lattice, no decorative spindles.
art_direction.silhouette: A hexagonal mill floor sprouting a forest of cogs at two clearly different heights, four furrowed millstones standing around its rim and one crank with a knurled handle in among them — an ironworks seen from the gantry.
art_direction.part_vocabulary: gear_low is a squat toothed puck whose teeth start at the floor — teeth DOWN; gear_high is the same tooth ring carried at the top of a plain smooth column, so it reads as a lamppost with teeth UP in the air and a bare shaft below; gear_tandem is a full barrel of teeth from floor to pin top, the tallest toothed thing on the board and obviously the piece that can touch both heights; mill_gear is a full-height gear crowned by a dressed grinding disc cut with radial furrows, topped by a prism hub with three, four, five or six sides — the hub prism is a player's identity for the whole game and is read by counting flats, never by colour; crank_gear is the only piece with an arm and a knurled knob, and the only one bearing a direction arrow; grain_pellet is a small smooth domed washer with no teeth at all, so a score piece can never be mistaken for a game piece.
art_direction.surface_treatment: 1.2mm-deep radial furrow dressing (the harp pattern of a real millstone) across every mill_gear crown; 1.2mm raised sills ring the eighteen outer pins to mark yard positions where a mill or the crank may stand; 1mm raised plank ribs run across the board floor between pins so the yard reads as a floor rather than a jig plate; 1.2mm raised arrow and knurl on the crank cap; 1mm chevron water-texture on each sack_spindle base and on the granary_bin's front.
art_direction.hero_shot: Straight-down overhead mid-grind: a hand on the knurled crank knob, a chain of low gears running away from it, a stand of tall high-tier gears alive on the other side of the yard doing nothing this round, three millstones docked on the rim with their furrows catching the light, and four spindles of stacked grain washers at visibly different heights.

components.name: yard_board
components.desc: Hexagonal slab, ~230mm corner to corner, ~12mm thick with a chamfered skirt. 37 integral pins (8mm diameter, 30mm tall, generous 0.5mm running clearance to gear bores) on a triangular lattice at 30mm spacing — centre, ring of 6, ring of 12, ring of 18. The 18 outer-ring pins each sit inside a 1.2mm raised sill marking them as yard positions, the only pins a mill_gear or crank_gear may stand on. Floor between pins carries 1mm raised plank ribs. Fits the P2S bed in one piece.

components.name: gear_low
components.desc: Low-tier gear: 12 teeth on a 30mm pitch circle (~35mm outside diameter), teeth band occupying the LOWER half of the pin height starting just above the floor, ~10mm face. 8.6mm bore, three round lightening holes in the web for grip, chamfered tooth crowns and generous backlash so a long train turns freely by hand. Meshes only with another gear_low, or with a full-height piece, on a neighbouring pin.

components.name: gear_high
components.desc: High-tier gear: the same 12-tooth, 30mm-pitch ring, but carried at the TOP of a plain smooth column so the teeth occupy the UPPER half of the pin height and nothing but bare shaft sits below. Same bore and clearance. Meshes only with another gear_high, or with a full-height piece.

components.name: gear_tandem
components.desc: Full-height gear: the same tooth profile run the whole pin height as one barrel of teeth, ~28mm face. The only supply piece that meshes with both tiers, and therefore the only supply piece that can weld the two halves of the yard into one machine — or into one seized lump.

components.name: mill_gear_tri
components.desc: Millstone, three-sided hub. Full-height tooth barrel like gear_tandem, crowned by a dressed grinding disc cut with 1.2mm radial furrows; the crown does not overhang the tooth circle, so it never fouls a neighbouring pin. A triangular prism hub rises from the crown as a finger grip and as its owner's mark.

components.name: mill_gear_square
components.desc: Millstone, four-sided hub. Identical to mill_gear_tri apart from the square prism hub.

components.name: mill_gear_penta
components.desc: Millstone, five-sided hub. Identical to mill_gear_tri apart from the pentagonal prism hub.

components.name: mill_gear_hex
components.desc: Millstone, six-sided hub. Identical to mill_gear_tri apart from the hexagonal prism hub.

components.name: crank_gear
components.desc: The only power in the box: a full-height tooth barrel with a solid cap carrying an offset arm and a 14mm knurled knob standing 22mm proud, plus a 1.2mm raised arrow showing the clockwise driving direction. The only piece in the game with an arm.

components.name: grain_pellet
components.desc: Score piece: 15mm-diameter, 5mm-thick domed washer with a 9mm hole, smooth and untoothed so it can never be confused with a gear. Threads onto a sack_spindle rod; a stack's height is the score, readable across the table.

components.name: sack_spindle
components.desc: Score post: 40mm round base, 1mm chevron texture on its skirt, with a 8.5mm rod standing 62mm tall — capacity 12 grain_pellet with room to lift the top one off with a thumbnail.

components.name: granary_bin
components.desc: Open bin, ~70 x 50 x 25mm, thumb scallop cut into one long wall, 1mm chevron relief on the front. Holds the grain_pellet supply within reach of every seat.

setup.text: Set the yard_board in the middle of the table with all 37 pins empty. The 18 outer pins are ringed with a raised sill: those are the YARD PINS, the only pins a millstone or the crank may ever stand on. The other 19 pins take supply gears only.

Put the whole gear supply in an open pile beside the board where every seat can reach it: 14 gear_low, 7 gear_high, 3 gear_tandem. Anyone may take from it on their turn, and what is left in the pile is the game's clock.
Fill the granary_bin with all 28 grain_pellet and set it beside the board.

Each player takes one millstone — the hub prisms have three, four, five and six flats, and the one you take is your mark for the whole game — and one sack_spindle, which stands in front of their seat, empty.

Choose a first player any way you like; they are the start player of round one and play passes clockwise. Starting with them, each player in turn stands their millstone on any empty yard pin. Then the start player stands the crank_gear on any still-empty yard pin.

turn.text: MESHING (the fact the whole game runs on). Two pieces on neighbouring pins mesh only if their teeth are at the same height: a gear_low meshes with a gear_low, a gear_high with a gear_high, and a low never touches a high. A gear_tandem, a millstone and the crank_gear all carry teeth over the full height, so they mesh with anything on a neighbouring pin. Pins that are not neighbours never mesh, whatever stands on them.

POWER. Each round opens with the start player either lifting the crank_gear onto any other empty yard pin or leaving it where it is. This is the strongest move in the game: the crank drives only what it can reach through meshed teeth, so its pin decides which part of the yard runs at all, which tooth height is alive, and which way every millstone will end up turning.
ACTIONS. Then each player, beginning with the start player and going clockwise, takes exactly one action: PLACE, SHIFT or PASS.
PLACE. Take one gear of any kind from the supply — gear_low, gear_high or gear_tandem — and stand it on any empty pin, yard pin or inner. Then test it, below.
SHIFT. Instead of placing, lift your own millstone off its pin and stand it on any other empty yard pin. You may not put it back where it came from. Then test it, below.

TEST FOR A BIND. Immediately after a PLACE or a SHIFT, turn the crank_gear a quarter turn by its knob, and nudge one gear in every separate cluster the crank cannot reach. If anything refuses to move, you have closed a loop containing an odd number of meshes and the yard is BOUND — an odd ring of gears physically cannot turn. That move is illegal: take the piece back (a placed gear returns to the supply, a shifted millstone returns to the pin it left) and your turn ends with nothing done. You do not get to try again.
PASS. Do nothing this round. A player with no legal action must pass.

THE GRIND. When everyone has acted, the start player turns the crank_gear one full turn clockwise, the way the arrow on its cap points, and everybody watches the millstones. Every millstone that turns CLOCKWISE earns its owner one grain_pellet from the granary_bin, threaded onto that player's sack_spindle. If exactly one millstone turned clockwise this round, its owner takes two pellets instead of one. A millstone that turns counterclockwise, or does not turn at all, earns nothing.

DIRECTION (the other fact). Meshed gears turn opposite ways, so a millstone grinds clockwise exactly when an ODD number of gears stands between it and the crank_gear along the chain that connects them, and turns backwards when that number is even. A millstone meshing straight into the crank is therefore the worst-placed one on the board, and two millstones on neighbouring yard pins mesh with each other and can never both grind. Nobody has to count any of this: turn the crank and look.
Pass the start player role one seat clockwise and begin the next round.

end.text: The game ends at the end of the round in which the last gear leaves the supply pile.

It also ends at the end of any round in which no gear was placed at all — everyone shifted or passed and the yard stopped growing — and at the end of the round in which the granary_bin is emptied of grain_pellet. Whichever comes first, that round's grind is played out in full before the game stops.

win.text: Compare sack_spindles: the tallest stack of grain_pellet wins, and it is tall enough to judge from across the table without counting. If two or more stacks are level, the win goes to the tied player whose millstone turned clockwise on the final grind; if that still does not separate them, they share the win.
